Who Should Own Your Domain, Hosting and Website Accounts?

Decide which website accounts your business should own, what access a provider needs and what must be handed back when the project ends.

By SiteSutra · 25 October 2026

← All articlesYour next step ↓

A business can approve a website and still be unable to manage it. The domain may sit in a former provider’s account, renewal notices may reach an old email address, or search and hosting access may depend on one person who is no longer available.

Account ownership belongs in the website brief before design or development starts. The goal is straightforward: the business keeps control of its essential assets, while each provider receives the access needed to complete an agreed job.

Separate ownership from working access

An owner can control users, billing, recovery and important settings. A contributor or manager may be able to do the daily work without controlling the entire account. The exact role names vary by provider, so record both the person who owns the account and the permission granted to everyone else.

Use an email address controlled by the business for the primary owner where the service allows it. Add the developer, marketer or agency through named user access instead of sharing one password. This creates a clearer handover and makes it possible to remove access without rebuilding the account.

A practical ownership starting point
Asset or accountPreferred business controlProvider access to agree
Domain registrationThe business or authorised proprietor is the registrant and receives renewal notices.Limited access or a supervised DNS change when needed.
DNSThe business knows the active provider and can recover the account.Permission to add or change the records named in the scope.
Hosting and deploymentThe business can see the plan, billing, domains and current deployment.Deployment access appropriate to the agreed release workflow.
Website sourceThe final source and repository location are documented.Contributor access with the review and release rules recorded.
Business emailThe business controls the mailbox, recovery and billing.No mailbox access unless a specific support task requires and authorises it.
Search and analyticsThe business retains an owner or administrator role.Only the reporting or configuration role needed for the project.
Business ProfileAn eligible business retains primary ownership.An authorised representative is added as a manager or appropriate owner.
Forms and bookingThe business controls the receiving address, calendar and subscription.Configuration access limited to the agreed integration and tests.

Treat the domain as a business asset

ICANN describes the registrant as the individual or entity that registers a domain and enters into the registration agreement with the registrar. The registrant manages the domain through that registrar and has responsibilities under the agreement.

Record the registrar, registrant, renewal date, billing owner, recovery email and whether automatic renewal is enabled. Keep recovery details current. A website provider can help configure the domain without becoming the long-term registrant.

The domain and DNS may be managed in the same dashboard or by different providers. Write down both. Before changing nameservers or DNS records, record the current values and the reason for the change. Email, verification and website delivery can depend on those records.

Keep verified search access with the business

Google Search Console distinguishes owners, full users and restricted users. Its permissions documentation says an owner has full control and can manage other users, while full and restricted users have narrower rights.

The business should retain a verified ownership method it understands. Add a provider with the minimum useful permission for the agreed work. At handover, review users and verification tokens rather than assuming that removing one visible user removes every ownership method.

Search Console measures search visibility. Access to it does not prove rankings or enquiries. Keep the verified property under business control so future providers can compare evidence without creating a replacement property.

Use roles instead of transferring a local profile unnecessarily

Google’s Business Profile role guidance says a profile can have multiple owners but only one primary owner, while managers can handle many daily tasks without managing users or removing the profile.

For an eligible local business, the business should understand and retain ownership. Google’s ownership guidelines for authorised representatives say representatives should encourage the business owner to own the profile and add representatives as managers. Do not create or claim a profile using invented locations, hours or business details.

Give reporting tools deliberate roles

If analytics is configured, record the account and property, collection purpose, administrator, implementation owner and people who can view sensitive commercial data. Google Analytics documents administrator, editor, analyst and viewer roles in its account structure guidance.

Do not grant broad administrator access merely because someone needs to read a report. Similarly, do not leave the business with view-only access when it is expected to control the account. Confirm privacy and consent requirements for the actual implementation rather than treating account ownership as permission to collect everything.

Hypothetical example: a Varanasi professional practice

Imagine a fictional Varanasi practice commissioning a new five-page website. This is an original planning example, not a SiteSutra client engagement.

The proprietor registers the domain using the practice’s maintained business email and records the renewal details. The developer receives access to configure the website and deployment. Search Console is verified under the business-controlled account, and the developer is added with the role needed to review indexing.

The booking provider connects to a calendar owned by the practice. The developer tests the public booking journey but does not become the permanent calendar owner. The practice keeps the source repository, domain and hosting register, while the provider’s access and launch responsibilities are documented in the proposal.

At handover, both sides review the register. The practice confirms that it can sign in, reach billing and recovery settings, see the deployed website and identify the next renewal. The provider’s ongoing access remains only where a support arrangement requires it.

Ask these questions before work starts

  • Which account already exists, and who can currently recover it?
  • Which business-controlled email should receive ownership, billing and renewal notices?
  • What permission does the provider need to complete the scope?
  • Who approves domain, DNS, production and tracking changes?
  • Where will source files, licences and editing instructions be handed over?
  • Which recurring subscriptions continue after launch, and who pays them?
  • When will temporary users, tokens and test accounts be reviewed or removed?

If a provider must create an account during delivery, the proposal should say who becomes the owner, which email is used and how recovery is transferred. “We will manage everything” is incomplete without an asset list and an exit route.

Make the account register part of acceptance

A handover is complete when the business can use the agreed assets, not when a list of links is sent. Test access with the intended owner. Confirm the live domain, deployment, source location, form destination and booking calendar. Record support boundaries and the process for urgent changes.

Do not store passwords, recovery codes or secret keys in the register. Record the account owner, service URL, role, recovery contact and where the credential is securely managed. Share access through each provider’s controls.

Download the website account register

Download the website account ownership register (CSV). It includes starting rows for the domain, DNS, hosting, source repository, business email, Search Console, Business Profile, analytics, form delivery and booking calendar.

Every row begins with “Not reviewed.” Replace the examples with verified account information, but keep passwords, recovery codes, private customer data and secret tokens out of the file.

Keep ownership separate from performance claims

Correct ownership makes maintenance and measurement possible; it does not guarantee search rankings, AI citations or enquiries. Review search visibility in the verified search property. Record AI citations, if sampled, with the dated prompt and cited URL. Review qualified enquiries from real received messages or bookings against service fit.

Put ownership into the website scope

Add the account register to the project brief before development begins. Name the owner, provider role, approval point, recurring cost and handover evidence for each essential service.
